newsitem.title: JAPAN: German revaluation may hurt credibility - OECD.
newsitem.headline: German revaluation may hurt credibility - OECD.

text.p: Germany's decision to revalue its central bank assets could hurt the country's credibility heading into European economic and monetary union (EMU), the deputy secretary-general of the OECD said on Saturday.

In an interview with Reuters Financial Television, Kumiharu Shigehara said he was not sure why Germany chose to implement the plan now, but the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) will be watching its effects on Europe.
"All I can say at this stage is that credibility is crucial in all respects of the efforts towards monetary union," Shigehara said.
A German government plan to revalue its official reserves came under heavy criticism last week as critics warned the scheme could hurt the launch of a single European currency.
The Bundesbank, Germany's powerful central bank, rejected Bonn's plan, which is aimed at bolstering government finances.
Shigehara added that the OECD will be watching European public opinion closely and if the revaluation plan lessens Germany's credibility, he would be "seriously concerned".
Shigehara said a shift in opinion about Germany could improve the prospects of other countries trying to join the EMU, such as Italy.
He also said there is room to interpret EMU criteria, and that the "spirit" of the Maastricht Treaty should be followed.
He cited as an example the provision that countries must achieve deficit-to-GDP ratios below three percent.
"If the budget deficit, after adjustment of the cyclical position, is well below three percent, that must be taken into account rather than the overall budget deficit numbers," Shigehara said.

Sustainability of consolidation is also important, he said, adding that if Italy, or any country seeking EMU entry, were to meet the criteria this year but not next, that would be more damaging than not meeting it in either year.
He added that it does not make sense to exclude a country for being slightly below the target.

That said, European governments need to pursue fiscal consolidation more aggressively in the long term, Shigehara said. This could reduce long-term interest rates which would be beneficial to investment in the region, he said.
But in the short term, Europe must make labour and product reform a priority, he added.
Once European economies lose the ability to adjust to regional shocks through their exchange rates, it will be vital that they be able to adjust through price and wage flexibility, he said.
"And in that respect, unfortunately, European countries have not been up to the requirements for the European Monetary Union," he said.
